title: Piecewise Point Evaluation at an Isolated Boundary
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
question:
Given the piecewise-defined function
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 3, & x < 2 \\ 11, & x = 2 \\ x^2 + 4, & x > 2 \end{cases}$$
what is the exact value of f(2)?

options.explanation: Incorrect. This evaluates the left branch 2x + 3 at x = 2, ignoring the strict inequality x < 2.
options.misconception: Student evaluated the left branch formula 2x + 3 at x = 2, ignoring the strict inequality x < 2 and overlooking the isolated point rule explicitly defined at x = 2.

options.explanation: Incorrect. This evaluates the right branch x^2 + 4 at x = 2, ignoring the strict inequality x > 2.
options.misconception: Student evaluated the right branch formula x^2 + 4 at x = 2, ignoring the strict inequality x > 2 and assuming right-sided limits determine function values.

options.explanation: Correct! The piecewise rule explicitly specifies that when x = 2, the function output is 11.
Incorrect. The point x = 2 is explicitly included in the domain with assigned value 11.
options.misconception: Student observes that the left-hand limit 7 and right-hand limit 8 do not match, mistakenly concluding that a jump discontinuity means the function value itself is undefined.

explanation: To evaluate a piecewise function at a specific input x = c, one must locate the branch condition that contains c. Here, the condition x = 2 is explicitly assigned the value 11. Therefore, f(2) = 11, regardless of the values approached by the adjacent branches as x approaches 2.
